title: Geometric mean of two positive definite matrices as unique positive Riccati solution
expression_sketch:
Let A and B be positive matrices in the sense of Bhatia (Hermitian positive definite n x n). Define
  A # B := A^{1/2} (A^{-1/2} B A^{-1/2})^{1/2} A^{1/2},
where every square root is the unique Hermitian positive definite square root. Then (Bhatia Theorem 4.1.3):
  (i) A # B = B # A;
  (ii) A # B is the unique positive definite solution of the Riccati equation X A^{-1} X = B;
  (iii) A # B = max { X = X^* : [[A, X], [X, B]] >= 0 }.
If AB = BA the formula collapses to A # B = (AB)^{1/2}. The inverse identity (A # B)^{-1} = A^{-1} # B^{-1} and det(A # B) = (det A det B)^{1/2} are recorded in the surrounding discussion.
latent_structure: One MATRIX_FUNCTION master, the congruence formula A^{1/2}(A^{-1/2} B A^{-1/2})^{1/2} A^{1/2}, is simultaneously the unique positive Riccati solution and the maximizer of the block-PSD order. Commuting versus noncommuting is one object: the geometric mean reduces to the ordinary product square root precisely on the commuting stratum.

function_domains.principal_square_root_on_HPD: Unique Hermitian positive definite square root of a Hermitian positive definite matrix (Higham Corollary 1.30; Bhatia uses this unique positive square root throughout the geometric-mean formulae).
function_domains.geometric_mean: A # B defined by Bhatia (4.10) / Theorem 4.1.3 for a pair of positive matrices.

nonzero_conditions.statement: A and B are positive definite, hence nonsingular, so A^{-1} and A^{-1/2} exist (Bhatia Theorem 4.1.3: 'two positive matrices'; the Riccati form X A^{-1} X = B uses A^{-1}).
nonzero_conditions.label: DECLARED
nonzero_conditions.source: R. Bhatia, Positive Definite Matrices, Princeton University Press, 2007, Theorem 4.1.3 and equation (4.10)

positivity_conditions.statement: A and B are positive matrices, i.e. Hermitian positive definite (Bhatia, opening of Chapter 4 / statement of Theorem 4.1.3).
positivity_conditions.label: DECLARED
positivity_conditions.source: R. Bhatia, Positive Definite Matrices, Princeton University Press, 2007, Theorem 4.1.3

analytic_domains.statement: A and B are Hermitian positive definite n x n matrices. Then A # B is well-defined by (4.10), is itself Hermitian positive definite, and satisfies (i)--(iii) of Theorem 4.1.3.
analytic_domains.label: DECLARED
analytic_domains.source: R. Bhatia, Positive Definite Matrices, Princeton University Press, 2007, Theorem 4.1.3 and (4.10)

analytic_domains.statement: Every square root appearing in (4.10) is the unique Hermitian positive definite square root of a Hermitian positive definite matrix (Bhatia's standing convention for positive square roots; Higham Corollary 1.30).
analytic_domains.label: DECLARED
analytic_domains.source: R. Bhatia, Positive Definite Matrices, Princeton University Press, 2007, Theorem 4.1.3; Higham, Functions of Matrices, SIAM 2008, Corollary 1.30

branch_conventions: Positive square root means the unique Hermitian positive definite square root of a Hermitian positive definite matrix, not an arbitrary primary square root.
Bhatia's 'positive matrix' means Hermitian positive definite (Bhatia, Chapter 1 convention), not merely positive entries.

limit_domains.statement: The commuting reduction A # B = (AB)^{1/2} is stated for the stratum AB = BA inside the same theorem's surrounding discussion (Bhatia, paragraph after (4.10)), not as a limit of noncommuting pairs.
limit_domains.label: DECLARED
limit_domains.source: R. Bhatia, Positive Definite Matrices, Princeton University Press, 2007, paragraph after (4.10)

derived_conditions.statement: A # B = B # A follows from uniqueness of the positive definite solution of X A^{-1} X = B together with the inverted equation X B^{-1} X = A (Bhatia Theorem 4.1.3(i)--(ii) and the discussion immediately before the theorem).
derived_conditions.label: DERIVED
derived_conditions.source: R. Bhatia, Positive Definite Matrices, Princeton University Press, 2007, Theorem 4.1.3

public_source: R. Bhatia, Positive Definite Matrices, Princeton 2007, Theorem 4.1.3, DOI 10.1515/9781400827787. Origin: Pusz--Woronowicz, Rep. Math. Phys. 8 (1975) 159-170, DOI 10.1016/0034-4877(75)90061-0. Ando, Linear Algebra Appl. 26 (1979) 203-241, DOI 10.1016/0024-3795(79)90179-4.
why_not_cse_lgg: The congruence formula, the Riccati equation, and the block-PSD maximizer are three presentations of one matrix. CSE will not equate them, and will not reduce the formula to (AB)^{1/2} only on the commuting stratum. LGG will not invent the Riccati characterisation or the unique HPD square-root chain.
proposer_leak_risk: Hide geometric mean, Pusz--Woronowicz, Ando, Riemannian geodesic, midpoint. Catalog members are the expanded congruence A^{1/2}(A^{-1/2} B A^{-1/2})^{1/2} A^{1/2}, the Riccati X A^{-1} X = B, and the block-PSD maximizer.
notes: Positivity of A and B is written by Bhatia ('positive matrices' in Theorem 4.1.3); it is DECLARED from that theorem, not imported physical folklore. Do not insert an operator-monotone interpolation kernel or a general Fréchet formula. Do not replace the HPD square root by a non-positive primary square root. The commuting reduction is a special case inside the same definition, not a different theorem.
